utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Oric, I want to make sure, before we proceed, that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down, but I'm not receiving interpretation in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm hearing you now, but I wasn't hearing you before so I don't know what the accused said..

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused said the following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I follow the proceedings fully, and I understand everything in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning to Your Honours and good morning to my learned friends of the Defence team. My name is Mr. Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Joanne Richardson. And also you see at the table Mr. Jose Doria. He will become a trial attorney in the team acting in the near future as such, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it Jose or Jose? I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear with Mr. Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. May I ask first of all if there are any developments yesterday and which you had to verify, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not completely there with respect to the final result. However, our request unit confirmed that we did not receive anything. We're at this time seeking verification from Republika Srpska that they did not forward anything, and I think that would bring an end to the matter, whether or not we have records in this possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which case could you please then forward all the information to Ms. Vidovic who could then be put in a position to take it up with the person in Republika Srpska that gave her the information that everything had been supplied to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no comment on what the Prosecutor has said. I have information from the public prosecutor of Republika Srpska that these documents were set apart. I certainly wish to see those documents, whoever has possession of them, whether this Prosecutor or the prosecutor of Republika Srpska. I would now like to proceed with the witness. We have no other issues to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Do you have any other issues to raise, Mr. Wubben or Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In short, Madam Vidovic informed me this morning that the upcoming witness will take two hours. For me that was a kind of surprise, but she explained it to me. She can explain it further. It has to do with translation and taking the time for that. But it means that we might have some -- to do some rescheduling, because according to our projected scheme from yesterday and what Defence counsel confirmed to us, she planned to have around - it's always an estimation - one hour. But when it is two hours today, that will mean that the witness planned for this day to finalise has a chance to not be -- being completed today. So we will inform the Victim Witness Unit of this development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time yourselves do you require for the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours. And you need another two hours? So that's four hours. And how much longer do you think you need the current witness on the stand? How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best to finish as soon as possible. However, you saw yesterday that if I hurry, the interpreters cannot keep up. I'm afraid I will need about two hours. But I will certainly do my best, if possible, to be finished within an hour and a half. If you look at the transcripts, I always said that for this witness, Mr. Popovic, I would need two to two and a half hours. However, yesterday, when responding to my questions, I realised that this was a witness who takes up more time than usual because of the way in which he answers questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In rescheduling, perhaps you could consider eliminating Racine Manas from the list for next week. She is scheduled to testify on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that would spare you having to send back any of the other witnesses that you have lined up for that week. It's up to you. I'm not going to interfere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Of course. But that is a good option, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please stand up, Mr. Popovic. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are receiving interpretation properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will be resuming your testimony. As I explained to you yesterday, we hope to be over and done with it in the first part of this morning's session. May I just remind you of two things: First of all, that you are still testifying under oath in terms of the solemn declaration that you entered last Tuesday; and secondly, that the moment I notice that there is confrontation between you and Madam Vidovic, I will take all the necessary steps. I noticed you yesterday, how you were reacting at some of the questions that she was putting to you. She is here doing her duty. She has a responsibility towards her client, and you have to honour that. I told you on the first day when you came to this courtroom that your responsibility under the oath is to answer truthfully and fully each and every question that is put to you, irrespective of who is putting that question. I hope I have made myself clear and understood to you, and I hope that we will have less incidents and less confrontation than we did yesterday. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. And let's proceed with the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond cross-examination. May I also remind you again to allow for a pause between question and answer, since you speak the same language, because otherwise I will have problems with the interpreters who I have every intention to protect, as I explained to you yesterday. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic. I do apologise, Mr. Popovic. When responding to my questions yesterday, you said that your forces attacked Sandici with the intention of retaking some villages in the immediate vicinity of Sandici and which have been taken by the Muslims; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean, then, that these forces included volunteers from Serbia, the ones we mentioned yesterday, the ones you saw on that list?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about volunteers, because there were no volunteers in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's true, is it not, that these forces attacked the surrounding Muslim villages - I'm referring to the forces of Kravica - including Sandici in order to cleanse the terrain - I will use the same word you used yesterday - and to create something that could be annexed to Serbia; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is correct then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that we wanted to retake the villages of Mrantici Gornji and Mrantici Dornji, Jerkovici Golovi, those villages that had been attacked on the 26th and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, on the 29th, it was Sandici that was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Sandici that they were attacked on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic. Yesterday you told us, when the question was put to you whether you knew that certain persons that appeared on the list that was shown to you yesterday, the first 11, had died in Sandici on the 29th of January -- of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 29th of May. You immediately took us back to the 26th and said no, you should first think of what happened on the 26th because what happened on the 29th, three days later - you did precisely mention three days later - was in response to what happened three days before. And you did mention Sandici as a combat area on the part of the Serbian troops trying to regain possession of what they had lost three days before. So I take it that you are fully aware that there was some combat activity on the 29th, in Sandici, or in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I said that on the 26th, when it burnt, the army arrived from Bratunac to retake that village that had been burnt down. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Sandici burn down on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sandici?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. Let's move on. I will now quote to you a part of the statement you made to the Prosecutor in July this year. I think that yesterday you confirmed that in July of this year, you made a statement to the Prosecutor; do you remember that? Do you remember making that statement and signing it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now quote a passage to you. If necessary, I can show it to you. You said: "The village --"

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in paragraph 8 in the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said: "The village was defended on the front lines, and there were between 250 and 300 soldiers, including the logistics staff. After the siren went off, normally everyone who were to be on the front line took their positions." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous statement, then, you decidedly spoke about soldiers, not about the village guard, not about civilians who were keeping guard of some sort.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said soldiers who had to go to the line when the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he answered this, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that your father, your late father, was at the front line. What unit was he deployed in?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at Jezero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that answers -- answers the question. What's Jezero? Jezero is the name of a place, I suppose. But the unit, your question was --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, can you tell us precisely what you mean when you say he was at Jezero? What is this about? Because I asked you what unit he had been a member of, not at which position he had been.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Kravica, in the Kravica -- I don't know, there wasn't a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said of Kravica. Can you complete your sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence of Kravica, the village defence of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a Territorial Defence unit of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please tell us precisely what position your father held. At what position was part of the unit, or the unit of which your father was a member?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was at the defence line at Jezero, overlooking Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably found out when your father was arrested.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the time of his arrest, when was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning he went off to Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But in relation to the time when you last saw him, do you know when he was arrested? How long after that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrested at about 4.00 on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your testimony you said that your father was wearing a JNA uniform, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when asked by the Prosecutor about the attack on the 7th of January, 1993, you said when the siren went off, everyone went to the front lines. Is this because all able-bodied men had been mobilised? Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for clarification and to make sure that the record is correct, I believe the witness testified that he and others remained in the bakery. So it's not everyone. I think we need to be clear about this. The witness should be asked who went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a very proper objection to your question, Madam Vidovic. Could you -- I suppose I would direct it to the witness himself straight away. When you say "everyone," everyone without a single exception? For Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond example, did you go to the front line each time you heard the siren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were exceptions. When you said "everyone," it wasn't really everyone. It was several but not all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So who wouldn't go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Women, underage children, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you didn't go to the front line, and you're not a woman, you're not a child, and you're not an elderly. So why wouldn't you go, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was at the bakery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Were there others like you in the same position, who were not women, not children, not elderly, who couldn't go or who wouldn't go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Men didn't go to the front line if they were not fit. There were people working in the bakery, in the kitchen, in the rear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if someone just didn't feel like going to the front line, would there be consequences? If, for example, when your father heard the siren, instead of going to the front line he just decided not to go, was he free to do so? And if he did not go to the front line, would he have suffered consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had to go. When the line was attacked, people whose duty it was to defend the village had to go. And if they didn't, they had to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we've heard a lot of witnesses coming here who were in the village guard and who, instead of going to the front line, ran away and sought shelter to save their lives. So was that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they fled if they were elderly, children or women. But able-bodied men had to attempt to defend their village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But why? Was it because it was part of the army or the territorial force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they were defending the village. How can I put it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that, at least we have the impression, the village guard system was on a voluntary place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, the guard was, yes. But then when attacks on the villages began, then there was a line of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Vidovic, he's back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did other men also, who were able-bodied, receive call-up notes, just as you did?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your military assignment was the bakery, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How do you mean "military assignment"?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your military assignment, your duty at that time, your deployment, was it in the bakery?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that's the reason you didn't go to the front, because you were deployed in the bakery.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fighters in Kravica had received weapons, including automatic rifles; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, isn't it, that your father too signed for an automatic rifle with ammunition on or around the 7th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Nikolic, whom we talked about yesterday. You knew his sons too, I assume; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ratko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that his son Zoran also had an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about him, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had signed for any weapon whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now move on to something different. You handed over a document to the OTP yesterday. This document is a diary. I assume that you handed over to the OTP the original of that diary; am I right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly, then, did you hand over?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get to the bottom of this straight away. Who has the original, do you know? Don't look at Ms. Richardson. Look at me, please. Who has the original? You told us yesterday that this was found in a field, and that it was preserved and copies of it handed from one person to the other until it reached the Office of the Prosecutor and until it reached us yesterday. Do you know who has the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original is with my uncle Milic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Just one moment. With respect to the record, I noted that counsel indicated that the witness handed over the document yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, it's all right. But these are petty, petty things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I know. I just wanted for the transcript, Your Honour, for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's not waste time on that. But have you ever seen -- Ms. Richardson, has any one of you seen the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We have not, Your Honour. And the witness is saying that his uncle has a original. I don't know if he knows this for a fact or if he's assuming what what his uncle has is the original. It could be very well a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think we are not dealing with a stupid man. We're dealing with an intelligent man, young enough to have complete control of his memory, who can distinguish between a copy and an original. The only problem we could have if the interpretation that he's receiving does not translate properly, original and copy, which I don't propose is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we have this original? Would your uncle be prepared to make it available? And then we will hand it back to him, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the name of your uncle again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radovan Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you taken note of it, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have, and we will make arrangements to collect this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I think we have surmounted that problem, and at least we know where the original is. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to this very issue, I just wanted to clarify who is in possession of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what you know about when this diary was found. What were you told?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary was found in 1996 or '97, when a work platoon who were working on the power lines found this book in a meadow. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was out in the open, just lying there.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what my uncle told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that after the genocide in July 1995, the Muslim population left the area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Srebrenica, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this document was exposed to the elements and bad weather, just lying out there in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on what it was left on the meadow, Madam Vidovic. It could have been left there on purpose in anticipation of the workmen passing through that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before I move on, I would like to ask the OTP to immediately present this document so that we can inspect it, or rather as soon as they receive the original so that we can inspect the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure they will, Madam Vidovic. I don't need to remind them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that your father was wearing a uniform. The other soldiers in Kravica too were, in fact, wearing uniforms, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of uniforms were those?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The jackets and trousers that were normally worn by the JNA earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your house was in the vicinity of the school building in Kravica; am I right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that, from the 14th of November, 1992 onwards, the school building was being used as the command of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, also known as the Kravica Battalion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about its name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you did live and work in the immediate vicinity of the school building, didn't you? I understand that perhaps you're not aware of the name of this unit, but is it not true that this was the headquarters of the Kravica Battalion ever since the Bratunac Brigade was first established?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they referred to it as the staff or headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us, describe for the Chamber, what exactly was there in that building, in addition to the kitchen that you have described?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a kitchen. I got flour from a room there; that's where the food was being kept. But I didn't go into any of the other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you also said that the headquarters was there too. What was it, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four or five people there, who were there in Kravica, who were distributing food and whatever else was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, Witness, that in the school building, the only people who were there were people who were distributing food, or were there other people there too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December, when Glogova was cut off, there were about 20 soldiers there who came to help out when Kravica was surrounded. There were 20 soldiers from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this the Panthers unit from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what they were called, but they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Outside the school building in Kravica, they were there at the time you are talking about, weren't they? That means December 1992. There were tanks too and APCs captured by the Muslim forces on the 7th of January, during the attack; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many tanks and APCs you mean. Which amount exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any tanks at all, or APCs for that matter, outside the school building in Kravica in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one. I'm not sure what I should call it. People came across the hill, those who arrived in Kravica in December, and they drove it up there. It was some sort of an APC, something like that. It stayed right there, and it burned down outside the bakery, in the school yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a tank too?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the Praga? Do you know what a Praga is?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can tell him what it is, and perhaps he can give you an answer, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Praga is also a piece of heavy artillery which looks much like a tank.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said about those people who came from Bijeljina, that was the vehicle they used to reach Kravica in December. I don't know if it was a tank, a Praga, a self-propelled machine-gun or a transporter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did that vehicle have a machine-gun mounted, or something that could be used to fire?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not correct that there were mortars positioned near the school building too, mortars that the Muslim forces captured on the 7th of January, 1993? You should be in a position to know that, shouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the school, or anywhere in the vicinity of the school, there were certainly no such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where, then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that you saw no attackers; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see anyone set fire to the houses, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you only saw the houses burning in Marici, Jezestica, Siljkovici, and Brezak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your earlier statements, or rather, your statement to the OTP dated July 2004, you never mentioned that anyone had told you about the Muslims burning the houses. Would I be right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you mention it yesterday, then? You never mentioned it before in your statements, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I recalled some days ago that there was a man from Kravica who told me that they had been setting fire to houses and stealing food from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When exactly were you told this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as this man had left Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you not mention that in your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no time, and there were a number of people around. We didn't have enough time to really go through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you not agree, Witness, that on that day in Kravica and the surrounding hamlets, before Serbs left Kravica, there had been fierce fighting between the attackers and the various units stationed in Kravica, including the Panthers that you referred to a while ago.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean between those two parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I mean. They were firing at one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I wanted to object to what counsel has referred to as the witness confirming Panthers were involved. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did not confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: He did not .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I'll try to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there fighting between the attackers and the soldiers who were at Kravica, including the people from Bijeljina that you said had arrived in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. Between the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question for you. Is it not true, Witness, that on the 7th of January, the morning of the 7th of January, before the Serb forces, or the people you refer to as people carrying weapons in Kravica, everyone, including the people from Bijeljina, that these people fought the Muslims, the attackers who attacked Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is all getting very confusing. Let's go through slowly because otherwise it may end up meaning more than one thing. It's being put to you, Mr. Popovic, that on the 7th of January, when the village of Kravica was attacked, okay, the Serbs forces -- the Serb forces had already been fighting the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The village had already begun to fight, to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's before the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 7th of January, on Christmas Day, when the village was attacked, people went out to the front line to defend the village, and those people who had fled too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But was there fighting before the attack, or did the fighting start when the attack, or after the attack started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know that people left to go to the front line immediately when the attack started, Christmas. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Madam Vidovic, I think that answers your question. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does that not mean that during this fighting, damage could have been caused to the houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting from Marici, shooting at Kravica. The school building around my house, they started firing at Kravica from Marici, at the schoolhouse and the bakery. And when I said that some people were wounded that evening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Shooting from Marici, how far is Marici from Kravica - let's repeat that first - as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the crow flies, about 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when you say there was shooting from Marici, what kind of shooting? Were artillery pieces being used, or was it just small weapons, rifles and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was used. Among all that shooting, you couldn't even hear, you couldn't distinguish. It was coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And who was doing this shooting from Marici in the direction of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could it have been the Serbs themselves who were shooting from Marici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: When you told us that there was shooting from Marici, do you mean that the shooting, the shoots -- the shots have been fired in Marici, or do you mean that the shots came from the direction of Marici? Do you see the difference? The first would be that the shots have been fired in Marici to Kravica, or did you mean that the shooting came from the direction of Marici but the shots have been fired closer to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marici fell as soon as it was attacked in the morning. Our defence retreated to Siljkovici. They took Marici up to below OKA. And then they fired from the wood in the direction of Kravica. It was about 50 metres in the direction of Kravica from the wood, from Osoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs from Kravica return fire? Did the Serbs from Kravica fight the attackers?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, or rather, in the statement you made in July 2004 to the Prosecutor, you said that a decision had been made that the Serb army should retreat from Kravica; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To retreat, yes. They had already been broken up. They had to retreat. Everything was beginning to burn.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you answer my question. Who made this decision? Evidently you knew about the decision, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody made the decision. The village had fallen, it was over. Who would issue a decision about withdrawal when everything had fallen? Jezestica, Kajici, Siljkovici, Marici, Jezero, Brezaci, Mandici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. In your statement, you said: "We arrived at Opravdici and I saw hills -- I saw down the hills houses burning in Marici, Jezestica, Siljkovici, and Brezak." My question is: Is it possible to see from Opravdici houses burning in Marici, Jezestica, Siljkovici, and Brezak? What is the distance between the hamlet of Opravdici from Marici, Jezestica, and Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Marici to Opravdici, as the crow flies, it's not more than a kilometre. Between Opravdici and Siljkovici, there's a kilometre and two or 300 metres. The furthest is Jezestica, and this was about two and a half to three kilometres away. Kajici is right underneath, about a kilometre and a half. And as for Brezak, it's hardly 500 metres, as the crow flies. All the villages that I listed can be seen from Opravdici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that the configuration of the terrain is such that, in the village of Marici, the houses are in a valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where -- just a moment, Witness. Where are the houses in Marici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The biggest house in Marici, it's a two-storey house, and you can see it from Kravica, from the school yard, from the center of Kravica, near the community centre, near OKA. From all the places in Kravica you can see this biggest house in Marici, and you can see other buildings around it, the outbuildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the houses in Marici are in a valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No? Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has answered that question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct, Witness, is it not, that only a few houses in Siljkovici are on the slope facing Opravdici, and that the other houses are on the opposite side of the slope.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From Opravdici you can see at least five or six houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the other houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other houses are below them, but you can see the smoke, thick smoke, when they were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So they're not on the other side of the hill, the other slope?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are only two houses from Siljkovici. That's Lazarici, Lazarici, just two houses which you couldn't see from Opravdici, because they're in a valley. But you can see all of Siljkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on this, Madam Vidovic. At the end of the day, what is it going to change?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope we shall see this on the ground, and that's why I'm putting these questions. I apologise, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, in your statement, you said that your grandfather, Risto, didn't want to leave Kravica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't. He was 72 years old. He couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not correct that he remained in Kravica with a machine-gun, and that he was killed shooting at the Muslims from a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grandfather?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grandfather couldn't see across this room, let alone fire from a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your father fought -- was fighting with the Muslims near the school at Kravica when he was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was fighting at the line in Jezero. And when they started pulling out, he was unable to pull out and he was captured alive in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that the attackers of Kravica were Muslim forces under the command of Naser Oric. You do not know who ordered the attack on Kravica, do you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, who ordered the attack on Kravica. But I do know, when I got back to the village --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'll come to that. Just please answer my questions. I'll come to when you returned to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but I don't know that the witness -- the completion of his answer would have given additional information with respect to the command, and I'd like the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair objection. Would you finish your statement, Witness. You were asked the following question: Very well. You mentioned that the attackers of Kravica were Muslim forces under the command of Naser Oric. You do not know who ordered the attack on Kravica, do you? And you answered: I don't know that, who ordered the attack on Kravica. But I do know, when I got back to the village, and you were then interrupted by Madam Vidovic. Could you please finish that sentence: "But I do know, when I got back to the village ..." What were you going to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I got back to the village, on our houses in Kravica, there was graffiti saying "Naser Oric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of the graffiti saying "Naser Oric," you drew the conclusion that he was in command of that attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had no other reliable information about this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now move on. I will now ask you something about the identification of your late father. You did not recognise your father's body on your own, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when the autopsy was conducted. I arrived later on. When I got there, I asked to see the doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In fact, Dr. Zoran Stankovic showed you the body and suggested to you that this was the body of your father before you even looked at it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Moreover, yesterday you said that he suggested to you that you shouldn't even look at the body; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said I should remember my father the way he had been.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you of the statement you made to the Prosecutor this year. In paragraph 19, you said: "When I went to Srebrenica, I was told by the pathologist from Belgrade, who exhumed my father's body, that he had found my father's body and he showed me the body of my father and also explained that there were several fractures in his skull, thoracic cage and arms." You've just told us that you did not attend the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to take over the body, he was in a body bag. The doctor opened it and showed me everything. His front teeth were missing --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody said that you identified the body, that would not be correct, would it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That you recognised, that you identified the body as the body of your father.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw my father because he had a gold tooth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll come to that question. Witness --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me say this: I recognised it by his trousers. He had the military trousers on, and he was naked to the waist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, I don't know how you conduct cross-examinations in your country, but let's come down to the bottom of this all. Do you have any doubt at all that the body that you were shown in Srebrenica was that of your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the body of my father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are absolutely sure about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What makes you so sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had a gold tooth; he had his trousers that he had on when he was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he have any other mark, particular mark, that you could see on the basis of which you could identify your father? He had been dead for how long now? When he was shown to you, how much after his death was this? Yesterday you told us that he -- when at least you were told when he died, and now it's how much later that you've seen his body after the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995, in September or October. It was October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's almost two years later, almost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have to put another question to the witness in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement to the Prosecutor in 2004 that you recognised your father by his gold teeth. Yesterday you said something different, you said gold tooth. Please, can you describe your father's teeth precisely, as they were before his death?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father had one tooth in his upper jaw which was here. [Indicates]. This is where he had a gold tooth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you see gold teeth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I just think that this line of questioning regarding the word "tooth" or "teeth" is really not helping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I honestly don't know where Madam Vidovic thinks she is getting, but anyway, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see any record of the on-site investigation. We have contradictory statements. This witness said something different in his previous statement, and it's my duty to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it not correct that many people in that area have gold teeth? This is not something exceptional.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know who has gold teeth? I know that my father had a gold tooth, and I know it was there. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that many people who were killed were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Madam Vidovic, that the witness is not going back home with any doubts as to whether the person he saw on that table there was his father or not. You haven't changed anything, and I think we've lost a good quarter of an hour on this matter. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the pathologist gave you a piece of paper found on your father's body; is this true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you kept this piece of paper until recently and that you lost it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I couldn't find it when I was getting ready to come here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's not true, in fact, that this piece of paper was ever given to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true that Dr. Stankovic never gave you that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he didn't give it to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question. Again, please, I will not allow you to put the same question three times or four times, Madam Vidovic. He's answered that question, and Dr. Stankovic will be coming in any case and you can put the question to him as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were someone else to say that this piece of paper had been given to someone else and not true, then it wouldn't be true, I guess, would it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the one who kept this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Nego Eric was Slavisa Eric's grandfather. They were from Kravica, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were not telling the truth when you were describing the body of Nego Eric from Kravica and when you said that he had a piece of wire tied around his neck, as you said in your statement of 2004. And you said yesterday a piece of iron.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same, where I come from, a piece of wire or a piece of iron.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true at all that Nego Eric had anything - wire or a piece of iron - around his neck at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is true is that the cause of death of Nego Eric was that he was killed by a firearm; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. How can he confirm this to you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness stated yesterday that he was the one who found Nego Eric's body, and I have my reasons for asking this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He cannot certify the cause of death, can he? He cannot certify the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still know people that were shot in the head -- in the body and they still carried the bullets inside and they are still alive today, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown photographs of some houses. Would I be right in stating that some of the houses that you spoke about yesterday and which you identified were not in Kravica at all but in some other villages; Kajici, for example?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All of those houses are, in fact, in Kravica. Kravica, Grujic's house -- well, if you show me a photograph, then I can tell you again, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just explain where Stanoje Grujic's house is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to see the ERN -- one moment. The ERN, yes. For the record, the witness is being shown a photo which bears the ERN number 0108-7886, and which was tendered into evidence yesterday. Yes, you can now answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This house belongs to that person. It's between Kravica and Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you something else now, Witness. How many houses were there in the local commune of Kravica, including the hamlets that you marked? What's your estimate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including all the hamlets, I can't say exactly, but I think between 800 and 1.000 houses, including all of the hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We only saw some of those houses yesterday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the houses that you were shown in these photographs, you did not, in fact, see that any of those had been damaged on the 7th of January, 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house that I've just looked at, it burned down on the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm asking is whether you personally, in fact, saw the house burn on the 7th of January, with your very own eyes. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in no position to see. I had fled. I saw smoke rising from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So you saw those houses on about the 17th or 18th of March, 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could gather from your testimony, you were not present in the area between the 7th of January, 1993, and the 17th of March, 1993, were you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you not agree with me that anything might have happened in the meantime? Anyone could have caused damage to those houses, couldn't they, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw all those houses from up on the hill. I saw them burn from Opravdici, from Ocenovici. You could see Kravica clearly from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is, did you, in fact, see precisely those houses that you identified while they were burning?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean personally, with my own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. It is true, isn't it, that in this period of time, between the 7th of January, 1993, and the 17th of March, 1993, civilians were allowed to take construction material from those houses in order to repair their own houses, weren't they? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 7th of January and the 16th -- sorry, can you repeat the dates, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 7th of January and the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Kravica had not even been liberated. How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mean Serb civilians only, I mean civilians. Generally speaking, is it possible that construction material was being taken off those houses and carried off by people? I'm not speaking about Serbs only. Muslims civilians, for example, to repair their own houses. That's my question. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I know there was smoke rising. Kravica was all in smoke. I'm not sure whether they were taking anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you were a soldier with the army of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You do know that Serbian forces fought fiercely in this area in January, February, and March 1993, in order to regain control of this area, do you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in the area when this was being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you, in fact, Witness, throughout this period of time, between the 7th of January, 1993, and the 17th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Kravica fell, I left for Ljubovija. I left Ljubovija to go to Sabac to stay with my aunt in May. And I stayed there until Kravica was liberated, and then four or five days later I came back and --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. How was Kravica liberated? Was it liberated in combat?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That means you took no part in combat there; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the photographs that you saw, was it possible for you to draw any conclusion as to when these photographs were taken? Do you have any knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the photos of the houses that were shown to me yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this question because my understanding was you said some houses were repaired, or some houses were added to. Do you have any idea when those photos were taken?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was probably summertime. The grass was tall and the corn had grown too; therefore, it couldn't have possibly been wintertime. Perhaps 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at one of the photographs from this set of photographs, P459, the photograph that ends in 898.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is being shown photo 0108-7898.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are familiar with this building. You said it was the OKA yesterday. It's the warehouse, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a farmer's cooperative, OKA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it not possible that this damage came about following the genocide in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How on earth should I know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you not agree with me, or did you perhaps hear, that between 1.000 and 1.500 Muslims were murdered inside that building using different kinds of weapons, including shells? Is that something that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard that something had, indeed, happened there, but I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this is, could this damage have been caused by shells exploding inside the building?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, move to the next question, because this is going to be resolved when the person who took the photo will be produced as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a photograph in which you identified Mr. Oric on horseback.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P460, can the witness please be shown P460.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the OTP to look at the weather conditions reflected in the photograph. Your reply was: "I can see snow, so this might have been taken in January." I put it to you, Witness, that it might as well have been February or March. It is true, isn't it, Witness, that back where we come from, snow sometimes lingers on until as late as April or May. It's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you can't state with certainty that this photograph was taken in January, of all months.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I should tell you. I know this is Kravica, this is the center of Kravica, it's all right here. I'm not sure if this was taken on the 7th of January or February. How on earth should I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I could conclude this set of questions here, and we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we've been talking about the 7th of January, 1993, so far. Your involvement in the war does not end there, on the 7th of January, 1993, does it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the 7th of January, 1993 onwards, you worked in different sections of the Bratunac Brigade, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, will you bear with me, please. My questions have a lot to do with the credibility of this particular witness and his potential bias.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For a while you worked as a courier in the command of the Bratunac Brigade; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that after that, you were assigned to the sabotage and reconnaissance platoon of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were never a member of the sabotage and reconnaissance platoon of the Bratunac Brigade, is that your testimony, Witness, throughout 1995.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. That is the more important part, really. It is true, then, that in May 1995, you were transferred and became a member of the military police unit of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you remained with the military police of the Bratunac Brigade until the end of the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Vidovic. Judge Eser's notebook is not -- got stuck; in other words, and he's not receiving any transcript now, any transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it working now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but he can follow along on mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were a member of this brigade in July 1995, were you not; and later, when members of this brigade killed thousands of captured Muslims in the area, were you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a military policeman in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Jankovic was your commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My komandir. Komandir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You took part personally in the massacre of Muslims, especially in July of 1995, did you not, in the Srebrenica enclave when over 8.000 Muslims were executed. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 1995, together with a group of military policemen of the Bratunac Brigade, at Potocari, in the DutchBat compound where thousands of inhabitants of Srebrenica tried to find safety, you were separating the men from the women and children, were you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were at the checkpoint in Potocari near the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were at the base checkpoint on the 12th of July, 1995, were you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the checkpoint in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion male children too were being separated, sometimes even those that were as young as 13 years of age, if they were able-bodied; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't us, the military police, who were carrying out this separation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that many of these people were killed in the immediate vicinity of the DutchBat compound, the UNPROFOR base, and that many women were raped there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were, in fact, one of the military policemen who were separating men, putting them on buses and taking them from Potocari to Bratunac. Many of them were killed along the way, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true that they were killed. It's true that the military police escorted those Muslims from the checkpoint in Potocari to the school, but it is not true that anyone was killed along the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you deported those Muslims from Potocari to Bratunac, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was another part of the question which you didn't answer, Mr. Popovic. Ms. Vidovic asked you in the first place: You were, in fact, one of the military policemen who were separating men, putting them on buses. Were you part of the military policemen who were separating men? That's to start -- that's question number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you part of the military policemen putting these men on buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what was your involvement in all this transportation of men, as you described, from Potocari to the school? What was your involvement? How do you fit in the whole story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our role was -- we were from 50 to 100 metres away from the place where they were being separated. Our role was to stand beside the road. And the Muslims passing by us boarded buses. Then we got onto the buses and escorted them from Bratunac to Potocari - that was the role - to the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You and a group of about 10 other policemen stayed to secure the Branko Radicevic primary school in Bratunac in which a large group of Muslims was put in the night between the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that the military police were there securing that with other armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, do you recall that you made a statement to the Bratunac police about these events? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher now to put on the ELMO the statement by Mr. Nikola Popovic of the 28th of August, 2003, to the Ministry of the Interior in Bijeljina, the police station there. And I ask the witness to look at page 1 of this statement. Page 1 gives you details.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Witness, please look at page 2, where it says, "Statement," and then look at line 8, and I will quote: "I remember that on the 12th of July, 1995, I was at the Potocari checkpoint. That day the citizens of Srebrenica came to the Dutch Battalion compound in huge numbers, and I think that many Muslims were there, I think 4.000 to 5.000 at the checkpoint in Potocari. We, the military police, had the task of taking in and providing security for these people, together with members of the Dutch Battalion. Since, at the time, I was a new member of the military police, I didn't know my colleagues except by sight. There were 10 or 15 of us, members of the military police, there. That same day we were ordered to separate the women, children, and elderly, who, according to plan, were supposed to be transferred by bus and freight vehicles from that checkpoint towards Kladanj, that is, to Muslim-controlled territory, and we acted in accordance with that order." Witness, this was your statement at the time. Now you have just told us that you personally did not carry out this separation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I personally did not carry out the separation of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you said in your statement that you acted compliant to the orders.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police, we were all there with UNPROFOR. We were together with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
