utterances.text: Very well. On the same page you said: "I and other members of the military police, about 10 of us, remained to secure the elementary school, that is, the prisoners, until the next day." This is your statement, is it not? You signed it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you were at the scene of the crime in Potocari, and then at the primary school in Bratunac, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you weren't, even after seeing this statement? Are you claiming that nothing happened in Potocari on the 12th of July, that there were no murders, no rapes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for a moment, I'd like to object to this compound question. I think there are at least three questions by the Defence. Maybe we could have him answer each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Ms. Richardson. Could you please go through these questions one by one, Madam Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you, on the 12th of July, 1995, at the scene of a crime in Potocari? Were you present at this separation of men and women?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's two questions. Separating men and women is not a crime in itself. So let's go through it. With regard to the separation, I think he has answered the question more than once, and he has denied having taken part in the separating. So if you are asking him now whether he was, on the 12th of July, 1995, at the scene of a crime in Potocari, you need to describe to him the crime that you are referring to, and then you ask him whether he was present at the scene of the crime, of that particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll put a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you were among the 10 or so persons securing the Branko Radicevic primary school in the night between the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police secured that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That same night, in the sight of many people there, together with another person in the school, you seriously mistreated an imprisoned teacher from the secondary school in Bratunac, Mr. Sirucic. Then you dragged him out of the school, and since then he has been missing.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, me?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that an authorised person from the Bratunac Brigade conducted investigations about 30.000 German marks and gold belonging to the teacher, Mr. Sirucic. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this investigation showed that you, with Mr. Carlton from Kravica, a student of Mr. Sirucic, took him to the nearby village of Voljevica, forced him to show you where he had buried 30.000 German marks and some gold, and the investigation concluded that you dug up this money and divided it among yourself; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, the 13th of July, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we move to the following day, do you have these documents relating to this investigation, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have them very soon. I have reliable information about this, and we will present this evidence in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now have some other documents to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the next day, the 13th of July, 1995, you were in the OKA warehouse, the warehouse we saw just a while ago, and there, in the presence of Jovan Nikolic, the then director of the warehouse who was previously the commander of the Kravica Territorial Defence, participated personally in the massacre of between 1.000 and 1.500 Muslims in that warehouse; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I don't like the way this is all being conducted. Were you ever summoned by anyone and asked questions about Mr. Sirucic and the allegation that you had taken part in the recovery of 30.000 German marks and some gold? Were you ever questioned on this by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is the first time I've heard this. I was all over the federation working with livestock, in Tuzla, in Sarajevo. I'm still working all over the place. And nobody ever has pointed a finger at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you've never been questioned about this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we have an investigation, I suppose, Madam Vidovic, that comes to a conclusion that the accused -- that the witness was involved, and this investigation supposedly will show that he was interviewed and really investigated. Okay, let's proceed. We are at the OKA now, and he has denied that he was ever involved in the massacre of 1.000 to 1.500 Muslims, together or in the presence of Jovan Nikolic. Is Jovan Nikolic still alive?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, he is, and he was on the witness list. However, he has been withdrawn. He was withdrawn just before the start of the trial. I would now like to ask the usher to put on the ELMO document -- a document which is a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document -- one moment, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This statement to the Republika Srpska ministry, you want to tender it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be marked as Defence Exhibit D124. Thank you. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to ask the usher to put on the ELMO the statement on facts and the actual plea agreement in the Momir Nikolic case, 02-65-T. And the relevant part is paragraph 9, and it relates to the murder of 1.000 to 1.500 Muslims in a warehouse in Kravica. And it's on page 5 of both versions, the second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I quote: "I established that among those who participated in these murders were: Nikola Popovic from Kravica, who was attached to the Bratunac Brigade Military police; Milovan Matic, who was attached to the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade; Ilija Nikolic, who was attached to the 1st Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade; Raso Milanovic, who was the commander of the Police Unit in Kravica. I also found out that the director of the warehouse, Jovan Nikolic, witnessed the execution." I will put a question to you in connection with this, Witness. You played a leading role in these murders, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are entering into delicate territory here. Witness, under our Rules, if you are asked questions, and if you answer -- if you are asked questions which, if answered by you truthfully and fully, would expose you or could expose you to criminal proceedings either here or elsewhere, you have a right ask us, the three Judges here, to be exempted from answering that question. So if there are any questions put to you that you feel, by answering them, you could expose yourself to criminal proceedings, you have that right, and you are free to draw our attention to it. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put a question to you. Have you heard that some people survived the massacre in OKA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. No, I haven't. I'm glad if they survived. Let them come and point a finger at me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please answer my questions. In the early autumn of 1995, the bodies of these people which had been buried with bulldozers in a mass grave were exhumed, and then they were moved and re-buried in another location. You participated in this as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the security of the military police, when that grave was dug, and I wasn't there then. I left the police when that was done. I was expelled from the police because, before that, I was at Trnovo, at the terrain, and we did not perform the tasks that were given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I move on to my next question, I tender this document and ask that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this will be D125.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else now. Do you remember that before this Tribunal, under oath, you testified in the case against Blagojevic and Jokic on the 23rd of June, 2004, as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me, Witness, please. You were then asked what you were doing on the 12th of July, 1995. You were asked the same questions I asked you today, and you replied that you had had a day off and that you were playing football in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to page 11072 of the transcript, the statement of Mr. Popovic of the 23rd of June, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote from this statement: "On the 12th --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We need to know the line, page, and everything before we can follow you, Madam Vidovic. Which page are you referring us to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 11072; the line is 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have that page on the ELMO so that the interpreters can follow, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence team asked you the following question: "On the 12th of July, the next day, could you please tell us what you did." And your answer was: "On the 12th of July, I was off. It was our big holiday, St. Peter's Day, so I was off. Question: All right. Well, what did you do on your day off?" And your answer was: "We had a soccer game." Please allow me, Witness. You spoke under oath then. What you said was not true, was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, listen, you have the rotation schedule for the military police in relation to that period of time. If you look at that, you will see exactly what we were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I showed you a statement you made to the Bratunac police a moment ago in relation to the 12th of July. I asked you questions about that. But now I will draw your attention to something else. You were also asked by Defence counsel at the time whether, on the 28th of August, 2003, you gave a truthful account of events at the police station in Bratunac, which you confirmed. You confirmed that the signature was, indeed, your own; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page, and which line, Madam Vidovic, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just add a couple of words in connection with this, because the same questions were asked by the OTP, and then I'll give you the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that the Prosecutor asked you as follows: "When you gave a statement to the police, was it a truthful statement?"

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't we have a right to be able to follow you while you are reading from the statement, please, or from this transcript? So could you please give us the page and the line number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 11099; 23, 24, and 25, the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was that your account was truthful. Mr. Popovic, this was a statement dated August 2003 which you gave to the Bratunac police, and you confirmed that the statement was truthful. Even so, the statement you gave under oath, the testimony, was a different one when you testified in the Blagojevic case, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what counsel is referring to at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she's referring to that in the statement of the 28th of August, he says one thing, while she's suggesting that on that day, he was, according to his testimony in Blagojevic, playing football, having his day out celebrating St. Peter's Day. I think that's what she means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's what she means. I mean, that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did on the 12th of May -- 12th of July, 1995, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 12th of July, I can't say for sure. I know about the 13th. The 12th was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the 12th St. Peter's Day, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was St. Peter's Day. And do you remember celebrating St. Peter's Day by having a day off, on which day you even played a soccer match in Milici, or wherever it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was in Milici. And I returned to the military police building where I spent the night. The next day I was in Potocari. On the 13th, it was Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we are saying that during the 12th, until 8.00 in the evening, he was having his day off. After 8.00, he was in the -- back to his post, in other words, where he was stationed. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the football match was over, it was about 4.00 or 5.00, I returned to the military police building. I spent the night there. And the next day I was assigned to Potocari. The Muslims came outside the UNPROFOR base in Potocari in great numbers, on the 13th, and from there transferred to Bratunac. On the 14th, the convoy left for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Madam Vidovic, I hand him back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago, in answer to one of my questions, did you not say that you spent the night between the 12th and the 13th of June, 1995 securing the Bratunac primary school where these people were staying? And now you're saying something different.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the evening of the 13th. On the 14th, the convoy set out to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Popovic, not only is that what you told us today, but you also told the same thing to the Bratunac police.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told the Bratunac police about the 12th in Potocari; however, it was on the 13th. And my statement was that I was in Potocari on the 13th when the separation took place. On the 14th, the convoy left for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. In that same case, under oath, on page 11071, line 11 through 13, you said: "A military bakery was set up, and this is where I worked until the fall of Kravica in 1993." When asked by the OTP yesterday, and I asked you the same question later on, you were not telling the whole truth, were you? You said that the bakery was catering for the local population. My question to you was, was it a military bakery, and your answer was no, it was a bakery catering for the local population. Here under oath you said something completely different; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bakery was for Kravica, and I worked there. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were not telling the truth, Mr. Popovic, were you? You were not telling the truth when you told us that it was a bakery for the local population. It was a military bakery, in actual fact, was it not, which you stated correctly in your testimony in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was catering for the entire village. How should I know whether it was military or civilian? But the whole village was using the services of that bakery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I hate to interrupt as much as I can, but you're dealing with three professional Judges. Do you honestly believe that by suggesting this to the witness, you could ever convince us that the witness is not telling the truth? Forget other things. But do you think that you are going to suggest to us or make us -- convince us that he is not saying the truth simply because it may not be clear whether this bakery was catering for the whole village or whether it was catering for the army or whether it was catering for this or whether it was catering for that. We are dealing with much more stronger stuff and much more important stuff. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you had 11, 12 jurors here, I don't know, it varies from system, and you were trying to impress the jurors, but it doesn't work like that when who is deciding are the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please believe me that my only intention was to demonstrate that the witness quite decidedly, in fact, stated that a military bakery had been set up in Kravica. This is a question which we believe to be extremely relevant, and that was the reason I asked the question, because the witness' answer was entirely different, even when I repeated the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you tell me what changes. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I know we're short on time, and I don't want to belabour the issue and the point you've already made. But this is not an inconsistency. The witness testified previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave that, Ms. Richardson. Let's not blow it beyond all proportions and reasonable proportions. We are just not on the same wavelength. I'm making it clear, we have this case in which your client is charged with particular events, and that's what we are going to concentrate upon. And a witness can be believed in whole, in part, or not at all. In other words, even if there is some inconsistency, even if there is contradiction with regard to what this bakery was, whether it was a communal, whether it was private, whether it was military, whether it was communal and then it became military, I mean, at the end of the day, even if he is -- if he is not consistent on it, at the end of the day, does it mean that he is not telling us the truth on other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one point. The point is not an inconsistency, but if a witness is consistently trying to underplay, understate, and minimise the military presence in Kravica, and that that's a thread which runs throughout his testimony, that's something which is very much important for Your Honours to be aware of. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, he has already testified that he himself was called and his assignment was in the bakery. He has already testified that there were troops who, at a certain point in time, came and gave a hand in the bakery. He already testified that the bakery was catering for many, including troops. And it goes on and on and on and on. You think we are going to care much about this particular matter that you have been dealing with? We are more interested in what is the crux of the case, whether the Prosecution, in other words, has proven the charges as they relate to Kravica, whether they have proven the charges as they relate to the death of his father, and that's it. We are not interested in all the other events. I mean, they may be relevant insofar as they may indicate whether we can believe this gentleman or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you honestly believe that this thing about the bakery is going to swing us right or left, you're pretty wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour. Of course we're not making a big thing of a bakery as such. We thought that Your Honours might be interested to see a pattern whereby a witness consistently understates the military presence in Kravica, when the charges relate to absence of military justification for an attack, you might bear that in mind when considering this witness' testimony, that he is consistently now trying to downplay the military presence. That's the point, Your Honour, and obviously we needn't dwell on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on that. Obviously I also remind you that he said that on that day they were cooking 50 pigs which was supposed to go also -- not just to the community but also the troops. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to respond to that. I believe the witness has been pretty forthcoming in the military presence, and I disagree that he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We don't need the Prosecution's comments on the witness. That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a comment -- I mean, the whole issue is not to entertain comments on whether the witness is -- from the Prosecution, whether the witness is truthful, reliable, or not. That is another matter which we will decide. What I'm trying to explain is let's not waste time, and let's distinguish between the chaff and the wheat and concentrate on the wheat, not on the chaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the purpose my questions was merely to establish the credibility of this particular witness. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-examination, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, this is not the first time you've heard about these allegations of your involvement in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Excuse me, what involvement in Kravica are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The Defence asked whether or not you were present and were involved in crimes committed in Kravica in July of 1995, and I believe this is not the first time you've heard about this allegation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is not the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified previously before this Tribunal, and you were asked about those crimes and you denied that you were involved or present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The Prosecution has accepted in a statement of facts an acceptance of responsibility which it has agreed with Momir Nikolic and the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- that this witness has been involved in crimes. If the Prosecution wishes to take a different position, then Carla Del Ponte herself should come here and the Trial Chamber in Momir Nikolic should be alerted that they have changed their position. They are estopped from taking this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I'm sure you know that what another indictee or accused says in relation to another person --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has accepted that this witness is involved in killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But they have accepted it as Momir Nikolic's version of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. They've accepted it as part of a plea bargain which is taken into account --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what? On the basis of that, in other words, on the basis of that, we can bring this person and condemn him outright.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You sit down. You sit down. You sit down. You sit down. You sit down. And if you behave like that, I will have to take steps against you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't given you the floor. I haven't given you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a short break, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We will not have a break for the time being, Ms. Vidovic. We will have a break later on, and you will explain to the accused that if he does that, I will have him restrained. I will have him restrained. I will not hesitate for a moment. I will not allow anyone to behave like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want his -- unless I give him permission to speak, to address the Court -- exactly, okay. I will cut off his microphone in any case, if he tries to speak without my authorisation. And if he speaks without my authorisation, I don't want anything on the transcript. Mr. Oric, if you behave like that, I will have you restrained, and you know what having you restrained means. Yes, Mr. Jones, what another person, what another accused has said in relation to this witness here has got nothing binding as regards this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My submission is that the Prosecution is estopped from taking this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution may have, not may have, certainly accepted the declaration of Momir Nikolic as a statement of facts that, according to him, happened on the events that he was making the statement about, but that's about it. It's very convenient for the Prosecution to agree. I can't imagine the Prosecution not agreeing to anything that was stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't nail the accused or make him a liar if he says, No, I was not involved in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I fear for the interests of justice, if the Prosecution is going to chop and change in each case. These are important matters of the killings of thousands of people, and surely the Prosecution should be consistent in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic could have mentioned anyone, as far as I'm concerned. At that point in time, do you mean to say that the Prosecution has no right to question these persons and say, This is what others have said about you? What is your position? And this is what is happening now. Do you think that the Prosecution would not have accepted and they would have told Mr. Nikolic, Now first we check with Mr. Popovic, next we check with Mr. X and with Mr. Y whether it's true that they were involved in these killings on such and such a day, and then we will decide whether to accept -- if someone is saying these killings took place, these persons were involved, I came to know about it, I was involved in this way, I was involved in that way, others were involved in this way and involved in that way, do you expect the Prosecution to say, We will not accept those?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a matter for them. But once they have taken that position, they are estopped from taking a different position. They should review the matter with the Trial Chamber which heard the case, they should review the matter with Momir Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to you, then, anyone who has been mentioned by Momir Nikolic must necessarily be prosecuted, charged and brought before this Tribunal by the Prosecutor because there is no question that what is mentioned by Mr. Nikolic can be untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, it's not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The legal argument is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sure they've promised immunity in any event to this witness. My point is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a suggestion which I will now ask the Prosecutor to make an announcement or a declaration upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. We were going to ask the witness. We were cut off before asking that question. If I may, Your Honour, as I said, it's a question of estoppel. But if the Prosecution has taken a position in one case, there is a collateral estoppel in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no estoppel. I am sorry, you are mixing the two issues completely. You are mixing the two issues completely. If an indictee, if an accused, if a sentenced person makes a statement involving others, involving others, it doesn't mean that the Prosecution -- even if it is accepted by the Prosecution, it is accepted for the purpose and in relation only to that accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In interest -- Your Honours have referred in the past to the interests of truth and reconciliation of this Tribunal. If the Prosecution in one case says, Yes, Nikola Popovic was involved in killings; in another case they say, no, he's a perfectly decent, truthful witness; in another case they say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, you're mixing things up. What the Prosecution said in the Momir Nikolic case is that they accepted the declaration of Momir Nikolic that these events happened on such and such a day, and that these or those persons were involved in those events. Punto basta, that's it. It starts from there and it finishes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just feel that truth and reconciliation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can't move it from that to another case and, on the basis of it, either hold the witness responsible or bar the Prosecution from putting questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You have my submissions, Your Honours, and I won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there was a question about immunity or any promises made to this witness, and I would just like to state for the record that there were none, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to continue with my re-direct to the witness about whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, no, no, I'm sorry, let me take it a little bit further. Has the witness been interviewed or interrogated by the Prosecution in relation to those events?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: He has not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has not. I cannot ask you why he hasn't. Is he a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time he is not a suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, you testified previously that you -- when I said "previously," I mean when you came to the Tribunal in the Blagojevic case and you testified that you were not, in fact, involved in these crimes committed in Kravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And have you been charged by any local -- by the local authorities in Bosnia for these crimes committed in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the military vehicle that you observed in Kravica on the day of the attack, you said that this vehicle belonged to 20 soldiers from Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember if this vehicle was operable on the day of the attack? Was it being used during the attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It stayed where it had been parked. There was no one to start the engine running.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally, with respect to the picture you were shown and where you pointed out that Naser Oric was sitting on a horse, and with respect to the snow on the ground, was it snowing on the day of the attack on Kravica, January 7th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he answered that question yesterday or the day before. He said that there was plenty of snow. Whether it was snowing on the day or not is irrelevant. It's whether there was snow on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there snow on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there snow on the ground that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt would like to put some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Regarding that picture which was just mentioned, and the snow on the ground, you mentioned that you have seen a video where, more or less, the same group of persons occurred whereas the pictures were taken from another direction. That is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the center of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Now, on the picture which you were shown yesterday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary. Because there you could see the center, as you called it, of the Kravica on the same picture - you remember, probably - and you saw that it was completely burnt down. You saw the chimneys. Do you remember it or do you want to see the picture again? My point is, this picture could not have been taken on the 7th of January, the day of the attack, because the building was already completely ruined; it was not burning, it was not smoking any longer. So it must have been taken on a later date; do you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree it wasn't on the day that Kravica fell, but after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Good. That was one question I had. Then another one. I think to remember that when you explained what you have heard about how your father was captured by the Muslims, you said that you had heard that the men or man who found him was in some uniform. Do you remember your testimony here? What kind of uniform did you see that those people had who captured your father? I'm aware you were not there, but after what you have heard.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An American uniform, a camouflage uniform. Mijo Gavric was there; five metres away from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You don't mention any UNPROFOR uniform or something like that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, American uniforms. That's what we call camouflage uniforms. That's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I would like to come back to your statement with regard to the question of whether or not there was a cleansing or not. You use the term "cleansing." Was this a term that was already used in 1992, or was it a description which was phrased later on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "cleansing," I meant that our people from Kravica, who were travelling from Kravica to Bratunac, were killed on the Glogova road. And then on the following day we would go and search the terrain, because a lot of people were killed on the Bratunac-Kravica road, the Glogova road. A lot of people were killed. The Muslims would come behind their backs and ambush there. About 10 people were killed, including civilians. And that's what I meant to say when I said "cleansing." It was actually searching the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, "cleansing" was not a normal term before the war in the former Yugoslavia; it was a rather new term. Now, killing people, on the one side, or that people leave a village would, up to that time, not have been called cleansing. So was there special meaning connected with this word "cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I help a little bit? There is cleansing, meaning mopping up the terrain, but this is not the cleansing that you were referring to when yesterday you told us that, Yes, I remember that Glogova was cleansed earlier on in the year, and we actually referred you to May. When you said Glogova was cleansed earlier on in the year, you were then asked again further questions to explain what that meant. And basically you said that it was cleansed of the Muslim population. So the cleansing that Judge Eser is referring you to is ethnic cleansing and not mopping up of the terrain. And I am pretty sure that you know -- you're fully capable of answering Judge Eser's question. If you don't, obviously we're free to draw our own conclusions. But you're not dealing with children here, let's put it like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Would you like to answer this, my question, as it was interpreted by Judge Agius? What means "cleansing"? I mean, it cannot be identical with killing people or that people leave --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our parts, cleansing means mopping up, searching the terrain. Cleansing, you search the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. My second question refers to your statement of 2004, in July. It was already referred to by the Defence. In paragraph 8, you said: "The village was defended on the front lines, and there were between 250 and 300 soldiers, including the logistics staff." Now, what did you mean with this 250 or 300? Have there been only in Kravica, or were they distributed over a greater, a broader area? And what means "logistics staff" in this context?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistics means cooks, bakers, warehouse staff issuing food. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And these bakers and these people, have they been part of some sort of a unit together with armed people.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And these 250 to 300 people, have they been located only in Kravica, or did they control or defend a broader territory beyond Kravica? You showed us a long line going from Mandici, Siljkovici, and so on. Now, when you referred to 250, 300 people, did you refer only to Kravica, or did you want to say that all people taken together made up the number of 250 to 300.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say people who were defending the line. I assessed that there were between 250 and 300 people defending these villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: With "line," do you mean not only the circle around Kravica but also the whole line going from Kravica to Siljkovici, Jezestica, and so on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. My third question refers to the event where you have been confronted with the body of your father. And the Defence had referred to, and also the Prosecution the other day, that there was a paper handed over to you by the pathologist. And then you stated: "This paper was with me for years, but when I tried to find it last night, I could not find same," "this paper," I guess, was meant. Now, is it thinkable that you gave this paper to some other person?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was my mother or my sister who gave it to me. I know that I received this paper personally from the doctor who found it in his pocket, and I couldn't find it in the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And you have no explanation why you did not find it anymore?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't find it. When I return home, I'll look for it again. I know I did get this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And is it not thinkable that you gave it to somebody else, some other person outside of your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I gave it to anyone. This paper should be at my home. I can't remember giving it to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- two matters before this witness leaves. Firstly, in all the excitement, I think an exhibit number wasn't given to the transcript for Blagojevic and Jokic of this witness' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be given D126.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The second matter is simply that I would ask Your Honours to bear in mind that our client suffered a great deal during the war, and as a result of the 1995 genocide, lost a lot of family members and friends, and it's naturally a topic which is of great purport to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he must exercise restrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure that you will speak to him like all lawyers do during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. I simply ask the Court to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He must understand that I will not allow any nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not the first one I've had to deal with, and I am sure that he will not be the last one either. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's the first to have experienced a genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me it's almost a piece of cake, how to handle him. I'm making it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will be as rough as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I simply ask the Court to bear in mind the special circumstances of Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I bear in mind everything, actually. At this point in time, we are here to do justice, and everything will be borne in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Popovic, this brings your testimony to a close here. You will be escorted now by Madam Usher, returned to your hotel, and then you will be given all the assistance you require to enable you to return back home. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on my own behalf, I wish to thank you for coming over to give testimony in this trial. I know that you have been here for quite a few days. I am sorry that you had to stay here for so long. On behalf of everyone, I also wish to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, our next witness doesn't have any protective measures, does he?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking because he was mentioned by name earlier. So how much time do you require with this witness, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: To my estimation, two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And another two hours, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think that Madam Usher needs assistance, or what is happening? Yes, she is here. All right. I can see that this is going to be very easy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can I know what the witness said, please, from the interpreters. Did you hear him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said: Take it easy, daughter, one thing at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, take your advice as the best advice you can receive for your lifetime, Madam Usher. Witness, Mr. Miladinovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's me. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I am the Presiding Judge; my name is Judge Agius. To my right I have Judge Brydensholt from Denmark, and to my left I have Judge Eser from Germany. We are presiding over this case, and you are one of the -- look at me, please. Look at me please. We are presiding over this case against Naser Oric, and you are one of the witnesses that the Prosecution has decided to bring over. So my first duty is to welcome you to this Tribunal, and I also want to make sure, since I am speaking in English, that you are receiving interpretation in your own language. Could you please confirm that, first and foremost, before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all loud and clear. I thank the Tribunal for inviting me so that we can clarify who did what in the war, in the village of Jezestica, what they did a long, long time ago in World War II and their grandchildren now did again. I'm prepared to take an oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not -- please don't try to make our life more difficult than it already is, Mr. Miladinovic. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, something which is equivalent to an oath, a solemn declaration that, in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to help you make this solemn declaration. You may remain seated. You may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am going to start reading out this solemn declaration, and each time I stop, I want you to repeat the same words yourself. I am going to start now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I, Dragomir Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dragomir Miladinovic, from the village of Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father's name is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please repeat only the words that you hear from the interpreters, nothing more than that. So I am going to start again. I, Dragomir Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Dragomir Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the exact truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And only the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Miladinovic. That was your solemn declaration with us. You basically have taken an oath here that you will be testifying the truth. Now, before you start with your testimony, I want to explain to you what the procedure is. You are first going to be asked a set of questions by Mr. Wubben, who I understand you have already met, and then he will be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is the lead counsel for the accused in this case. Madam Vidovic is to your left. Your duty in terms of the solemn declaration that you have made is to answer all questions truthfully and fully, as much as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. Your solemn declaration does not mean that you can answer the questions of the Prosecution fully and truthfully but you have no obligation to answer the questions by the Defence truthfully and fully. You have also an obligation to answer all the questions put to you by the Defence truthfully and fully. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If, at any time, you need a break, you feel tired, please draw my attention and we will have a break. I think, Mr. Wubben, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, I will start with questioning you regarding your personal background, and you can limit your answers by telling us yes or no. Your name is Dragomir Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You were born on the 30th of August, 1934.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So whenever there are previous statements indicating that your date of birth was the 20th of August, 1934, that specific date is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You were born in Jezestica, where you lived for the rest of your life.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your ethnic origin is Serbian.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You have ever been a farmer, also in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you have, as a farmer --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I've always been a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you have, as a farmer, any cattle, livestock, also in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: 1992, let me see, I had oxen, a cow, pigs, livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In 1992, when the war broke out, you lived in Jezestica together with your wife and two of your sons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were those sons named Djordjo and Ratko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, are you illiterate? Can you write or read?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. Block letters perhaps a little, but not really. I can't read or write. I can read some block letters, and I have been to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, I notice that you're wearing glasses now. Is it correct that you can see clear enough to watch pictures --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- photographs? Did you wear --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Please, as for photographs, it is just not true. What was photographed, it's a huge village with 20 homes, and there are not even five or six photographs there. Therefore, it can't be correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, we can't go on like this. The Prosecution didn't bring you here to sit down and say whatever comes to your mind and whatever you would like to say. The Prosecution brought you here so that they put specific questions to you, and please answer those questions, nothing else. And then it will be the turn of the Defence to put questions to you. But we don't want any statements from you except in the reply to the specific questions that are put to you. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But may I be allowed to ask one question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three houses are there on a hill, but I can't see them on the photographs. They are no where to be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No, we don't have to go into that, then. I will no longer talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, we will discuss that only if you are asked questions on them. If you are not asked questions on them, we will not discuss them. Then at the end of your testimony, I might decide that it's the case of asking you whether you want to add anything or not. But it's far down the road as yet. So let's start -- let's continue with your questions. You were asking him about his glasses, spectacles, and whether he can actually look at photos and see what they contain, and I gathered from his answer that he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My next question, Your Honour, I will put to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you also need glasses to see clearly in 1992 or beginning 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Three years ago I had surgery on both eyes. I worked in the Red Cross. I didn't need this. I came home, and all of a sudden it happened and I had to have operations on both eyes. I worked in the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Miladinovic, because otherwise you are going to be here, I anticipate, at least another week, the way you are answering. The question was: In 1992 and the beginning of 1993, did you also need to wear glasses like you do now? And you just answer it yes or no. That's what we require of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have glasses then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that answers your question, Mr. Wubben. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next question is related to the village of Jezestica. Can you tell us whether or not it's situated in a valley.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: This village is partly in a valley and partly on two slopes, on hillsides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, how is the terrain around your village of Jezestica, including the hamlets? Is it hilly with woods? Or how far can you look?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: You can see on both sides, and you can even see the River Drina. You can see as far as Serbia; that's how far you can see. And we would call out to each other from one hamlet to another. You can call out and see. And there are other villages on all sides and there are woods and there's everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you lived in the hamlet of Tanici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct. That's correct, yes. I didn't go anywhere from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you -- can you mention any other hamlets in this village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: That's my village. It had 540 inhabitants, 120 households. We didn't divide it up. I know everyone by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to suggest to the witness any names of hamlets that you had in mind, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it correct that the hamlets included in the village, apart from Tanici, are Djermani, Jecmista, Kijevici, Rankovici, Vresine, Radukici and Potkonijice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Potkonijice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it correct that these are the hamlets of your village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Jezestica had 10 hamlets. In the middle we had a reading room. We would all visit each other's houses. It was a big village, a strong village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are those hamlets close to the center of Jezestica or far away? Can you give a kind of distance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: You're taking me back. The village of Jezestica, Kajici, Tanici, Rankovici, Radukici, Potkonijice, Vresine, and so on, all of this was a single village. Not a local commune but a village. Kajici was also the village. It was the village, but it's divided into hamlets. But that's not the proper address. The proper address was the village of Jezestica. You could get a letter from anywhere in the world at that address.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. But again, the question is, these hamlets, are they grouped like a pattern, a square, a circle, or what? Can you describe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an aerial view, a picture, a photo, that you could show us of the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why don't we leave it until we go on site and move to the next question, or to the break straight away. I think we'll have a break now of 25 minutes. We are going to have a short break, Mr. Miladinovic, give you a rest a little bit, and then we'll start again in half an hour's time. And then you will only answer questions for 45 minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need to take a break until daybreak, as far as I'm concerned. I'm here. I don't need a break until daybreak tomorrow morning. Only if you're bored. But if you want to, you can take a break, but not for my sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are definitely not bored. We are never bored here, Mr. Miladinovic. But there are many others who've been working here and who need a break. So we'll have a 25-minute break, and then we will resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, let's continue. And you'll regulate a little bit the proceedings, see when it's convenient for you to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will do, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miladinovic, in the village of Jezestica, you stated that there were around 500 inhabitants. These inhabitants of the village, were they of Serbian origin, ethnic origin, I mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs. There was one Croat; the man was killed, and he has a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, how many houses were in the village, including the hamlets? Can you state that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: 120 households. All of that was Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And these households were mainly wood or stone or whatever construction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: The houses were built both of wood and of hard material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What do the people do in the area of Jezestica for a living, I mean mainly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: They lived by farming, keeping livestock. They also had plum orchards and other orchards. That was the only place I ever worked, and I built six houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it true that in 1992 in Jezestica, when the war broke out, that there were any attacks in that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: May I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. In fact, I think, Mr. Wubben, you need to help a little bit the witness, because if you tell him, Is it true in 1992 Jezestica, when the war broke out, that there were any attacks in that time, you can be specific. Could you tell us, Mr. Miladinovic, in 1992, what happened in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead and tell us. Go ahead and tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We need you to tell us what happened in Jezestica in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I tell you how it started? On the 5th of May, 1992, the hamlet of Bukova Glava, that's the village of Bijeceva, I went to have a beer because somebody was celebrating his patron's name on the following day, Djurdjevdan. I went to the village for that reason. In the evening, those 25 households were expelled, and they came to our village. That's how the war began. On the 20th of May, if you will let me talk about it, on the 20th of May, two people were killed, Mile Ostojic and Stojan Popovic. On the 20th of June, some houses were set on fire near Jezestica; two belonged to my son, and two to Radenko and Rada Miladinovic. After the 20th of July, there was an attack on Magisici, and this man who was married to a Croat woman was killed and so was Ljubica Milanovic. That was the 20th of June -- July, I apologise. Not June, July. On the 8th of August -- should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, witness, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the 8th of August, there was an attack on Jezestica by a commander at 11.30. I was there, and I'll tell you all about it. I don't have paper, but I do have a brain. At 11.30, there was an attack from Rankovici, and because this village is five kilometres by six kilometres, it's big, there was an attack on that village. They were burning houses, and a certain Zorga Bogicevic, if I had not arrived, would have been burned alive. I saved her because I was -- I was working on my land. I had wheat and I had oxen and I had livestock and I was looking after them. I was in the village guard. However, they started burning from Rankovici, Djermani, Jecmista. They were setting fire to all of that, but it came to where I was. I was at Mile Djukanovic's house, which was on fire. It was 20 metres away from where I was. Six or seven people were bringing jugs of water, but this was burning. And I said to them -- I fled. And when I came back, nothing was missing from my house, but everything else had been looted and the livestock driven off. We went off and came back in two or three hours. I discovered that Milan Rankovic had been killed, and I found the houses had been burnt. I found Sreten Rankovic. And again I went back to the field. What would I do up there? Down there I had three houses, and three were on the hill. My house had not been touched, nor my livestock, on that occasion. After that I went down into the valley, and Kijevici, Jecmista, and so on, there were two brothers, one's head had been split open. They were dragging them off to Bratunac. Their mother's throat had been cut. And then about nine people were killed; I can tell you their names if you want me to. Then afterwards we went back up there and we were keeping guard again. What do I know? I omitted to say that on Ilindan, in Glogova, a woman was burned alive in a car. Her name was Milenka Rankovic. It was always one person here, two people there. And then all of a sudden Borici, that commander, formed three fronts. People were being strangled. They would attack at 5.30 on Christmas. And one person was throwing things out of the house, and others were carrying them away in buckets --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt, but may I stop you because I have some questions related to this attack on Jezestica on the -- in August 1992. And I would like to ask you some more details, and please allow me now to put these questions to you. You told the Judges that you were in the village guard. When was this --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- village guard formed? Was that prior to the attack? And why was it formed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you that. My wife went to Cizmici, and Jevic said to me - Naser Oric knows him - he was married to someone from Potocari, and this woman's husband said to my wife, The time will come again when you will have to wear pantaloons to save your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And that was the cause of forming the village guards in your village of Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, that -- that was later, the guard was set up later. No, not then, it wasn't established then. But something was wrong. They knew this was going to happen, and we Serbs didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was this village guard formed on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I guarded my house and worked on my wheat. I was harvesting my wheat. I would be working in the morning and then harvesting in the afternoon. I didn't go far from my house. I had livestock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, you are a very important witness, and I suppose that you know that you have come here to try and help us -- and help us find our way in this search for the truth. I would like to invite you to try and answer the question that is put to you and not something else. The question that was put to you was a very simple one. You were referred to the village guard and asked whether the village guard was formed on a voluntary basis. And your answer was: "I guarded my house and worked on my wheat. I was harvesting my wheat. I would be working in the morning and then harvesting in the afternoon. I didn't go far from my house. I had livestock." But you didn't tell us whether the village guard was formed on a voluntary basis. So you said a lot of things which are not relevant to the question, and you never answered the question. This is why I'm trying to be as -- I need you to please try to answer the question and not tell us something else. Did you understand me? Because then the question has to be repeated, and that would mean that we are wasting or using twice as much time as we would need to. So I put the question to you, and just answer yes or no: Was the village guard formed on a voluntary basis, or was every able-bodied man bound to form part of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You don't know what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I was there to make sure nobody slaughtered our women. There were four of us there. One -- some of us were there in the morning and others in the afternoon. And when I was off, I went back to harvest my wheat. I never went far from my home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the question in a different manner. If you, for argument's sake, had decided you didn't want to form part of this village guard, were you free not to form part of the village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I had to, because otherwise somebody could have burst in and slaughtered our women. I had to tell them when to flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's another kind of necessity, then, that we're talking about. Yes, Mr. Wubben, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did the army instruct you to form a village guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did someone pay you for being a village guard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: They brought to the four of us, the women brought us money, to the four of us. I'm not trying to avoid saying that. I'm under oath. And up to 1993, after that I went to work in the Red Cross. I have documents, if you need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Miladinovic, thank you. My question is, did you, as village guard, wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you wear arms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: One of us had a hunting rifle, and when we changed shifts, when the two of us arrived to take up our shift, we would get the weapon from the other shift. So we -- the weapon was passed from shift to shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was there any equipment or military equipment given to you by the army or another force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were there military men --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, and the four of us, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Equipment" is a little bit of a very vast term that you're using, Mr. Wubben. Could you please be precise or even specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Any army equipment given to you or the other village guards by the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, my objection is to the use of "military" or "army equipment," which is so vast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine that this could encompass hundreds of items, possibly. So if you're referring to binoculars, ask him whether he was given binoculars. If you're referring to radios or other means of communication, put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were you given any support by an army in setting up these village guards?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You stated about the shift, the change via shift. Was this a kind of organisation like this, to post as a village guard in Jezestica during that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. I told you where I was, the four of us were there, right there, to prevent someone from coming from Poto -- we were on guard there in order to wake the women, and that woman I talked about who nearly burned alive. And now you're trying to sidetrack me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just trying to get more informations on behalf of the trial and the Judges to find out what's happening, and that's why I put forward these questions to you. Now, my next question is: There was a system of village guards. Was that done by a shift that you divided the taskings between each others, or was it organised on another way, in another manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose by --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, shifts, no. The two of us were there until midnight, or from midnight on. And there is a clock that we used, and someone would come at night, no one really acted as some sort of a shift leader. No one gave us orders, to the four of us who were there. Mico Ostojic, he was killed. Milenko Milanovic and Nikola Miladinovic; they are still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move on. Because at the end of the day whether there was shifts or no shifts, and whether this was part of the organisation, how much is it going to advance the case, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The next question, Your Honour, will then be:

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You stated to the Judges that they were setting fire to the houses, "they," during the attack. What do you mean by "they"? What did you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILADINOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said that. I saw -- I saw them burning. I recognised them burning things at 20 or 30 metres from where I was. 20 perhaps, not even 30. Seven or eight persons setting fire to things, carrying jugs and burning houses down. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
